sections.heading: A NEW USOTSUKI MII-KUN STORY?
sections.content:
Q: I'd love a new main-series volume or spin-off of Usotsuki Mii-kun to Kowareta Maa-chan.

A: Something should be going up on the website next month, probably.

sections.heading: MISTAKEN IDENTITY
sections.content:
Q: Why do you keep getting mistaken for a Gunpla-Ou judge (in the SF volume, in Yuiitsu no Negai, and so on)?[ref:gunpla-ou]

A: I really don't know why. I've also been mistaken for a theater troupe member before — someone once asked me, "Tsuruko came by recently, right?" She didn't.

sections.heading: THE POPULARITY POLL RESULTS
sections.content:
Q: Could you please publish the popularity poll results below third place... at least down to tenth? No, even fifth would be fine... please...

A: The results down to fifth place were already posted on the website.[ref:popularity-poll]

sections.heading: NAMING A CHILD
sections.content:
Q: Like Adou, I have a name I'd rather not use in front of other people. What kind of name would you give a child?

A: Nothing specific comes to mind right away, but I'd want to give a child a name that wouldn't cause them any inconvenience. I wouldn't want to be a burden to them.

sections.heading: BECOMING YOUR EDITOR
sections.content:
Q: What would it take to become your editor? Please tell me, since that's the goal I'm aiming for.

A: If you end up working at the Dengeki Bunko editorial department, let me know, and I'll request you by name.

sections.heading: DO YOU HAVE A GIRLFRIEND?
sections.content:
Q: Do you have a girlfriend?

A: What kind of question is that?! What am I supposed to do with that?! If I answer seriously — it's not impossible, is it?

sections.heading: ON SPIN-OFFS AND ANNIVERSARY SHORTS
sections.content:
Q: Are you the one writing the scripts for Chibi Yashiro-sama?[ref:chibi-yashiro] Usotsuki Mii-kun to Kowareta Maa-chan took first place in the popularity poll — if Denpa Onna to Seishun Otoko had won instead, had you thought about what kind of story you'd have written for it?[ref:special-short-story] Also, regarding File.2, "Well, It Was Bound to Happen Eventually," from the Super Iruma War project — did Niwa Makoto not end up going to university? The phrase "four or five years after graduating high school" has been bothering me. I'd really love to read the special Super Iruma War booklet that came bundled with Shinsekai, but is there really no way left to get a copy? I'm glad it's up on the official site, but I'd like to hold the physical thing in my hands and read it.

A: Most of it is stuff I came up with — ah, I mean the Chibi Yashiro-sama material. I honestly haven't given much thought yet to what a Denpa Onna concept would even look like. Also, yes, Makoto did end up going to university, probably. As for the booklet... how should I put it. Since it was never sold separately, that might be a bit difficult. I'll check with my editor about it.

sections.heading: WRITING APPEALING FEMALE CHARACTERS
sections.content:
Q: Your work moved me, so I want to try writing light novels too, but I just can't come up with girls who have that kind of endearing quality. How do you create such charming female characters?

A: I'm happy you find them charming, but I don't do anything especially deliberate for it... That said, writing appealing girls really is important in light novels, so I'd suggest reading a lot and studying how it's done. One approach might be to list out the traits you personally find endearing in a girl, then try combining those elements together. Though if you pile on too many traits at once, it tends to fall apart.

sections.heading: WHAT IS ART?
sections.content:
Q: What do you think art is?

A: Something that lets people easily understand the way another person's consciousness takes shape.

sections.heading: CHARACTER ORIGINS
sections.content:
Q: Who are the characters in your books based on? Yuiitsu no Negai, which came out in November, was really interesting! Though it might be a bit too grotesque for a first-year middle schooler...

A: They're not really based on anyone in particular. I don't have any real-life acquaintances I draw from at all.

sections.heading: A TAMAKO AND KIIRODORI SEQUEL?
sections.content:
Q: I'm a huge fan of Tamako to Kiiro-dori![ref:tamako-kiirodori] Is there really no continuation coming? P.S. Even getting to see a little more — no, a lot more — of Denpa Onna to Seishun Otoko would make me happy too!

A: Coming up with an unconventional game concept for that one is really hard, so a sequel might not be something to hold out much hope for... probably...

sections.heading: WHAT IS UNIVERSITY FOR?
sections.content:
Q: What do you think university is for?

A: It's a place to figure out what you're actually suited for. Not just academics or your career path, but also how you relate to other people.

sections.heading: WRITING FIRST-PERSON SCENERY
sections.content:
Q: When writing a novel from a single protagonist's first-person point of view, how do you describe the surrounding scenery using only the protagonist's internal commentary and narration? I'd love some advice on this.

A: Try reading it out loud as you write. If it sounds natural when you do that, then the description is working.

sections.heading: ON TOKAGE NO OU'S COVER ART
sections.content:
Q: I love every one of your series, but I've recently gotten hooked on Tokage no Ou. Really looking forward to what's next ^^ I'm curious what's going to happen to Ishiryuushi going forward, and I'm also curious about Namekuji's past and future... And out of everyone, I especially love Kawasemi-kun... will he never get to be on a cover?[ref:tokage-no-ou-covers]

A: Having a girl on the cover does tend to look better... but I'll put in a word with Buriki and my editor about it.

sections.heading: FUTURE ANIME ADAPTATIONS?
sections.content:
Q: Will Usotsuki Mii-kun to Kowareta Maa-chan and Tokage no Ou ever get anime adaptations?

A: An anime adaptation... I really hope so. But even if I say I want it made, if nobody actually makes it... I'll keep working toward making that happen!

sections.heading: CHOOSING AN ILLUSTRATOR
sections.content:
Q: By the way, how do you go about choosing the illustrator for your paperback releases?

A: It's always chosen by my editor.

sections.heading: ON DENPA ONNA'S BLANK SIX MONTHS
sections.content:
Q: Denpa Onna to Seishun Otoko is incredibly fun. My favorite scene is in volume three, when Makoto cheers Erio on during the practice match. On that note, I'd love to read a story about what happened to Erio during that blank six-month period that never gets written about in the books! Was she really scooped up the way Makoto imagines it in his delusion?[ref:erio-blank-months]

A: That's not really something I should spell out... maybe something strange happened, maybe it didn't — that part is sort of the liver of this particular work, so to speak.[ref:liver-metaphor]

sections.heading: UNABLE TO FINISH A NOVEL
sections.content:
Q: I'm a big fan of yours. Actually, I've been writing novels because I admire you so much. But while I'm in the middle of writing one novel, I end up wanting to write a different one instead, and I can never focus enough to finish anything. What should I do?

A: If you keep repeating that process, eventually you'll run into the novel you're actually able to see through to the end. Just be patient until then.

sections.heading: A CONFESSION OF ADMIRATION
sections.content:
Q: I like you so much it's honestly kind of painful, but what am I supposed to do about my heart racing like this?

A: That's way too embarrassing, so please don't ask the actual person that... but, um, thank you very much.

sections.heading: A FIRST-YEAR MIDDLE SCHOOLER'S DREAM
sections.content:
Q: I'm a first-year middle school student. After reading your work, I found myself thinking, "I want to write something like this too!" — and for the first time, I had a dream. So now I'm writing all kinds of stories. I already loved making up stories to begin with, so I've written quite a lot, but my writing itself isn't very good. Expressing things is difficult too, and it's been frustrating. What can I do to write the way you do?

A: No, it's probably better not to end up like me. If you make it into the finalist round of a contest, you'll get praised, and then rejected anyway for some reason or another. That part never changes, no matter how many years go by.[ref:iruma-contest-history]

sections.heading: A UNIQUE UPBRINGING
sections.content:
Q: I was born to a Martian father and a mother who brought a Tamatebako with her to their engagement.[ref:tamatebako] I'm thinking about submitting a novel to a contest. The entry requirements don't say submissions are limited to Earthlings only, so someone with my unusual background should be able to enter too, right? By the way, how many pieces did you submit the first time you entered a contest?

A: As long as you don't write it in Martian, you should be fine. And the first time I entered, I submitted... one piece.

sections.heading: MAN OR WOMAN?
sections.content:
Q: Are you a man? Or a woman?

A: I'm a boy — the kind with some backbone.[ref:scryed-quote]

sections.heading: ON ANGER
sections.content:
Q: I believe that among human emotions, anger is unnecessary — it's a feeling that doesn't need to exist at all. When I get angry myself, I end up feeling lonely, and when the people around me get angry, it just feels awful. I feel like my heart is slowly turning cold and withering away, and it's really painful. Does having that emotion actually let people do any good for others?

A: I don't think it lets you do good for others. But anger is my own driving force. It's the anger at things I can't accept that pushes me forward.

sections.heading: A DECLARATION OF A DREAM
sections.content:
Q: Please listen to my dream for the future (I'm a middle schooler) — is this a declaration? "I'm going to become a novelist!!!"

A: If you manage it, come join the Iruma Army.

sections.heading: WHEN WRITING GETS TEDIOUS
sections.content:
Q: After reading your work, I also want to become a novelist, and I'm working hard at it now. So here's my question: when you're in the middle of writing a story and you start feeling sick of it, or like it's become a chore, what do you do?

A: Since it's my job, I write it through to the end regardless. That said, the stuff I write in that state usually ends up getting scrapped afterward anyway. Funny how that works.

sections.heading: THE BARE MINIMUM TO BECOME A NOVELIST
sections.content:
Q: I also think it would be great to become a novelist someday. Please tell me what you think is the absolute bare minimum requirement for becoming one.

A: If it's the bare minimum, I'd say it's simply continuing to submit your work. You need to build up the ability to keep writing even after getting rejected. Do your best. ...By the way, I've noticed there have been a lot of "I want to become a novelist" questions this time around — for that kind of question, you might try asking the editor who appears on Web Radi instead.[ref:web-radi]

references.title: Dengeki Gunpla-Ou
references.note: In the afterwords of the SF volume of Denpa Onna to Seishun Otoko and of Yuiitsu no Negai, Iruma Hitoma mentions that people at his publisher's office have mistaken him for a judge of the 'Dengeki Gunpla-Ou' competition. He has also reportedly been mistaken for a comedian, a calligrapher, and a teacher of traditional Japanese dance — likely related to his distinctive personal style of dress.

references.title: Iruma no Ma First Anniversary Popularity Poll
references.note: In October 2012, to mark the first anniversary of the 'Iruma no Ma' website, the site ran a popularity poll covering all of Iruma Hitoma's works. The top two results were announced on December 10, and the top five were announced on December 25. This question was submitted sometime in that window, before the full ranking below fifth place had been made public.

references.title: Chibi Yashiro-sama
references.note: A four-panel spin-off manga illustrated by Buriki and serialized in Dengeki Bunko Magazine, centered on Yashiro, the mysterious alien character from Denpa Onna to Seishun Otoko.

references.title: Popularity Poll Bonus Short Story
references.note: As a reward for winning first place in the Iruma no Ma anniversary popularity poll, Usotsuki Mii-kun to Kowareta Maa-chan received a bonus short story written specifically for the occasion.

references.title: Tamako to Kiiro-dori
references.note: A novel by Iruma Hitoma published in July 2010, referenced here by a fan hoping for a sequel.

references.title: Tokage no Ou Cover Convention
references.note: Every cover in the Tokage no Ou series features the male protagonist, Ishiryuushi, alongside one female character. Kawasemi, a fan-favorite character the questioner is asking about, is male, and so has never had the opportunity to appear on a cover under that convention.

references.title: Niwa Makoto's Delusion
references.note: In volume seven of the novel, a delusion imagined by protagonist Niwa Makoto includes aliens retrieving their own kind from Earth — the scenario the questioner is referencing when asking whether the same thing may have happened to Erio during an unaccounted-for stretch of time in the story.

references.title: "The Liver of the Work"
references.note: Iruma uses the liver as a figure of speech for something quietly essential to the story's inner workings — an organ that does critical work without calling attention to itself.

references.title: Iruma Hitoma's Pre-Debut Contest History
references.note: Before his debut, Iruma Hitoma submitted work to numerous publishers' new-writer contests without ever winning one outright. One submission eventually reached the final round of judging for the Dengeki Novel Prize, sparking considerable discussion among the judges, but still came away without any award. That submission was later published as the first volume of Usotsuki Mii-kun to Kowareta Maa-chan.

references.title: Tamatebako
references.note: The mysterious box given to the fisherman Urashima Tarō in the well-known Japanese folktale of the same name, which unleashes old age on whoever opens it. The questioner invokes it as part of a tongue-in-cheek claim about having an unusual family background.

references.title: Scryed, Episode 12: "Kimishima Kunihiko"
references.note: The line quoted here ("A boy's got to have some backbone!") comes from episode 12 of the 2001 anime Scryed, spoken by the character Kimishima Kunihiko. It later becomes a defining line for the series' main character as well.

references.title: Dengeki Bunko's Web Radio Program
references.note: Iruma is referring to Dengeki Bunko's web radio program, which regularly features the well-known editor Kazuma Miki — who also happens to have been Iruma Hitoma's first editor.
